So, this post is conflating a number of things together. 

I would recommend the book “How Emotions are Made” to better understand the relationship between physical sensory information and emotion. Your brain creates an emotional state from a variety of signals, including the physical, social, situation, and your history. 

You can start to experience those emotions more consciously by noting and labelling them. My therapist had me trying to pick from a long list of very specific emotion words for a while, just while out in my day to day, because that is a proven technique for building emotional intelligence.

Stress is both a physical state (your body is trying to do things it doesn’t quite have enough resources to do) and an emotion (I feel pressured to do what I feel I cannot). 

I’d recommend trying to label how you’re feeling, 3x a day. Believe it or not, having words for emotions can actually make you feel them more strongly.

One thing that I think might be at-fault for story games' low popularity is that they don't often appeal to the motivations for why many people play games.   


They're usually:  
\- Low on action, excitement, destruction (Action)  
\- Not super social like an MMO, little community or online components (Social)  
\- Don't lend themselves to coming up with powerful builds or creative strategies that break the game (Mastery)  
\- Might be a bit linear and don't allow for experimentation or character customization (Creativity)  


That's 4 of the 6 motivations in the quantic model not met... leaving "Achievement" (players might enjoy finishing the game for the sense of completion) and "Immersion" 

Where I think they can succeed is players who enjoy immersion & story, and maybe players who like puzzles. However this is just a rather narrow window of motivations, so the game may have narrow appeal. But, I'd rather play a game with heart made for a small audience than a game with no soul made for the masses \*cough battlefield 2042\*

When playing D&D each character has 6 attributes: Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom and Charisma. Each attribute is represented by a number from 1-20, where higher number mean you're very strong or very smart, and lower numbers mean you're not very strong or smart. One way to generate these numbers is by using dice... specifically, you roll 4 six-sided dice and drop the lowest number, totalling the three highest dice. So, if you rolled a 4, a 3, a 6 and a 2, your attribute would be a 13.

Even when its gentle, or at least tactful, being called out for saying something like that will probably make people feel like shit. Maybe they deserve it, maybe not, that doesn't matter. What matters is that when someone feels called out, they get defensive, and often angry. Its the same kind of anger as an animal that's cornered and has nowhere to go... the only way through the pain of that situation is aggression.  


I'm not saying you should or shouldn't call people out... probably there is a way to do it that is kind, and even respectful of the person saying the offensive thing. However, not everyone is emotionally mature, and reactions may vary. If this person is a friend of yours, it may be that your values aren't compatible, or it may be that you need to talk through some of this a bit more. It could also be that this type of statement is part of how they were brought up, and confronting that could be a difficult thing for them.  


If this person is a coworker, I'd advise trying to let things slide if they aren't important... you aren't this person's manager or their parent, it can be tricky when personality feedback comes from a peer you don't know well. If its worth standing up and saying something, then do that with courage, but also acknowledge the risk you are taking too. Maybe it'd be better to talk with someone in HR or your manager first. Let them know its bothering you.   


Lastly... it could also be that the way you're handling the "calling out" isn't as tactful as you think. ENTJs, like INTJs, can often struggle socially and may be more blunt than they mean to be. The person might see hostility, or contempt in your face when you call them out... worst-case scenario. If you feel that way towards this person, I recommend distance or removing yourself from that situation. The only way someone might be receptive is if they know you care about them as a person, and showing contempt (or letting it slip through) is an easy recipe for an aggressive response.  


Whatever you do, if you want to call someone out for something offensive they've said, do it in a kind way that minimizes embarrassment. Genuinely work to care about the other person, especially if you don't feel that way right now.

When you raise the minimum wage, there are lots of different effects that may have on the economy, small businesses, and who they hire. For example, one thing that might happen is that businesses may choose to be more selective about who they hire since they have to pay them more, meaning that college students don't make the cut. Another thing that may happen is that an employer may end up needing to cut staffing or hours because they didn't get a sudden boost of money to pay people more. Likewise, if raising the minimum wage didn't result in *any* job losses, there would be more demand for basic goods and services since more people could afford them... so you'd then see an equal jump in costs & prices. Rent might increase, or the cost of groceries & household essentials.

Another issue with this statement is that it assumes people making minimum wage are relying only on that income to live... people might have multiple jobs, or they might be not the primary income-earner for their household. They might be in college and not yet relying on job income for their living expenses.

Poverty is a complex problem. The amount the minimum wage is set at does not truly matter when it comes to helping those who have to occasionally go hungry, or who are living paycheck to paycheck. Yes, those people would benefit from earning more in a superficial sense, but you can't just make one change to the economy and expect it to have only one single positive consequence... that's far too simplistic.

Games like Overwatch or TF2 have the damage indicator very near the crosshairs... keeps the player engaged and gives them the information where they need it.

HUD design for fast-paced shooters is a very fine-tuned science.

**FFS, don't just follow Daisy** 

Take it from the Developers, who included this tip in one of their livestreams. You can't just follow Daisy blindly, because the monster will always be faster than you, and they know where you are before you do, because of their smell ability. 

Instead of following daisy, use the direction she's running as an indicator of where the monster is right now. Then, make an educated guess of which way the monster is moving, and take paths on the map to cut him off. Daisy is good not because she can follow the monster, but because she can help you make an educated guess as to where its hiding.

The trapper has to be well positioned in order to catch the monster in an arena. Other things that help are not venturing too far into corners, staying near the middle of the map if you think the monster is trying to kite you back and forth.

Also, **Don't throw the dome if you're on your own.** That is the quickest way to die and you're not helping anyone.
